facts: A class defines a type of object with attributes (data) and methods (behavior); it is a blueprint, and each object built from it is an instance.
A class is a blueprint for creating objects.
Individual objects created from a class are called instances.
Each instance carries its own copy of the attributes, while the methods defined by the class are shared by every instance.

keyTerms.df: A class defines a type of object and serves as its blueprint.
keyTerms.eg: A class is used as the blueprint for creating objects.
keyTerms.mi: A class is an individual object created from a blueprint.
keyTerms.cx: The created individual is an instance; the class supplies the blueprint.

keyTerms.df: Objects are entities built from a class, with each one called an instance.
keyTerms.eg: Objects created from a class are individual instances.
keyTerms.mi: Objects define the methods shared by every instance.
keyTerms.cx: The class defines the shared methods, while objects are built from that class.

keyTerms.df: Instances are individual objects whose attributes are carried as their own copies.
keyTerms.eg: Each instance carries its own copy of the attributes.
keyTerms.mi: Instances define the methods that the class shares.
keyTerms.cx: Methods come from the class and are shared by its instances.

scenario.su: Students must classify a class and two objects as either a blueprint or instances before a deadline. They must also distinguish the separate attribute copies from the methods shared by both objects.
scenario.ma: class passage stating that it is a blueprint for creating objects, object passages identifying two individual objects created from the class, attribute observation showing each instance carrying its own copy, method observation showing class-defined methods shared by both instances

mc.q: An object is observed being built from a class, and the task is to label the class and the built object. Which comparison uses the source terms correctly?
op: Class is method; built object is class
Class is attribute; built object is blueprint
Class is blueprint; built object is instance
Class is instance; built object is method
mc.ex: The class serves as the blueprint, and an object built from it is an instance. Describing the class as an instance confuses the blueprint with the individual object built from it.

mc.q: Two objects have separate attribute copies and use methods defined by their class. Which account correctly connects the observed objects, attributes, methods, and class?
op: Instances define attribute copies and carry class methods
Instances create class methods and share blueprints
Instances share attribute copies and define class methods
Instances carry attribute copies and share class methods
mc.ex: Each instance carries its own attribute copy, while methods defined by the class are shared by the instances. Saying instances share attribute copies and define class methods reverses both stated relationships.

changeSummary: Re-authored both multiple-choice items to remove equivalent or partially supported distractors while preserving the source-grounded distinctions.
addressedDiagnoses: Addressed the diagnosed weak choice discriminability by making each distractor distinct and inapplicable under the cited claims.

facts: A user scenario is a narrative that situates a user type, motivation, context, goal, and tasks in a specific interaction.
Scenarios communicate a design idea through a specific interaction for a specific user.
A scenario should state who the user is, why and where they act, what goal they have, and how they pursue it.
Scenario work can reveal how needs vary with context and across diverse users.
Teams should validate and refine scenarios with the represented user group and collaborators.

keyTerms.df: A user scenario is a narrative distinguished by situating specified user elements within a specific interaction.
keyTerms.eg: A team writes who the user is, why and where they act, their goal, and how they pursue it.
keyTerms.mi: A user scenario communicates a design idea without situating a user type or context.
keyTerms.cx: The narrative must place the user type and context within the interaction, so those elements cannot be omitted.

keyTerms.df: A specific interaction is the setting through which scenarios communicate a design idea for a specific user.
keyTerms.eg: A scenario connects a specific user, goal, and tasks within the interaction.
keyTerms.mi: A specific interaction replaces the need to identify who acts and what goal they have.
keyTerms.cx: The interaction does not replace those details; the scenario should state the user and goal as well.

keyTerms.df: The represented user group is a participant in the validation and refinement of scenarios alongside collaborators.
keyTerms.eg: Teams ask the represented user group and collaborators to validate and refine a scenario.
keyTerms.mi: Collaborators should refine scenarios before the represented user group validates them separately.
keyTerms.cx: Both the represented users and collaborators belong in validation and refinement, rather than being assigned separate roles.

scenario.su: A team must classify a user scenario as stating or omitting the contents a scenario should state. Its decision is constrained to a narrative passage that states who the user is and why and where they act, plus a tasks notation that omits the goal and how the user pursues it.
scenario.ma: narrative passage stating who the user is and why and where they act; tasks notation omitting the goal and how the user pursues it

mc.q: A reviewer compares a narrative that situates user elements with scenarios that present a design idea; which distinction correctly describes the narrative and the specific interaction?
op: Narratives situate design ideas; scenarios communicate user types
Narratives communicate users; scenarios situate design ideas
Narratives situate elements; scenarios communicate design ideas
Narratives communicate contexts; scenarios situate specific users
mc.ex: A user-scenario narrative situates the user elements, while scenarios communicate a design idea through a specific interaction. Assigning the design idea to what the narrative situates swaps these relationships.

mc.q: A team compares scenario drafts before review: one records who, why, where, the goal, and its pursuit, while the others omit a recorded element. Which draft should it select?
op: Choose why, where, goal, and pursuit
Choose who, where, goal, and pursuit
Choose who, why, where, and goal
Choose who, why, where, goal, and pursuit
mc.ex: A scenario should state who acts, why and where they act, their goal, and how they pursue it. Stopping at the goal omits how the user pursues it.

changeSummary: Replaced the incomplete draft comparison with a constrained classification whose materials make the missing goal and pursuit inspectable.
Placed each uniquely supported assessment option first and updated each answer index to zero.
addressedDiagnoses: The revised scenario provides a supported decision because its passages make the omitted goal and pursuit directly inspectable.

facts: A demand curve shows the quantity of a good consumers are willing and able to purchase at each price, holding other factors constant.
Demand curves typically slope downward, reflecting the law of demand.
A change in price causes a movement along the demand curve, while a change in income or tastes shifts the curve.

keyTerms.df: A demand curve represents quantity consumers are willing and able to purchase at each price, holding other factors constant.
keyTerms.eg: For a good, consumers compare quantity at each price on a curve that typically slopes downward.
keyTerms.mi: A demand curve shows price at each quantity consumers purchase.
keyTerms.cx: The curve associates each price with the quantity consumers are willing and able to purchase.

keyTerms.df: The law of demand is the relationship reflected by the typical downward slope of demand curves.
keyTerms.eg: A demand curve that slopes downward reflects the law of demand.
keyTerms.mi: The law of demand is reflected when income shifts the demand curve.
keyTerms.cx: Income changes shift the curve; its typical downward slope reflects the law of demand.

keyTerms.df: Price is a value at which the demand curve shows a quantity consumers are willing and able to purchase.
keyTerms.eg: A change in price produces movement along a downward-sloping demand curve.
keyTerms.mi: A price change shifts the demand curve in the way a change in tastes does.
keyTerms.cx: Price changes produce movement along the curve, while changes in tastes shift it.

scenario.su: A reviewer receives a demand-curve sketch with a price-change annotation and a separate passage describing a change in income. Before review closes, the reviewer must label each as movement or shift despite their shared reference to the demand curve.
scenario.ma: price-change annotation beside movement along the demand curve, income-change passage beside a shifted curve, tastes-change notation beside a shifted curve

mc.q: A curve record shows a price change beside movement along the demand curve, while an income note accompanies a shifted curve; which distinction matches these observations?
op: Price moves along; income shifts the curve
Income moves along; price shifts the curve
Price and income move along the curve
Price and income shift the demand curve
mc.ex: A change in price causes movement along the demand curve, while a change in income shifts the curve. Treating income as movement and price as a shift reverses that distinction.

mc.q: A demand curve shows the quantity consumers are willing and able to purchase at each price while other factors are held constant, and it typically slopes downward. Which statement matches both features?
op: Shows quantity at each price; typically slopes downward
Shows income at each price; tastes cause movement
Shows price at each taste; income causes movement
Shows quantity at each income; price shifts curve
mc.ex: The demand curve shows quantity at each price while other factors are held constant, and it typically slopes downward. The income-at-each-price option also misclassifies a change in tastes as movement rather than a shift.

changeSummary: Re-authored the complete second multiple-choice item so one option uniquely matches both cited claims and the distractors are false or inapplicable.
addressedDiagnoses: Resolved the diagnosis that options 0, 2, and 3 were supported descriptions of the stated record.

facts: In the circular flow of income, money that households earn returns to firms as spending unless it leaks out of the flow as saving, taxes, or spending on imports.
Leakages are balanced by injections such as investment, government spending, and exports that add spending back into the flow.
When total leakages equal total injections, the circular flow is in balance and national income neither rises nor falls.

keyTerms.df: The circular flow describes household earnings returning to firms as spending unless they leak out.
keyTerms.eg: Money that households earn returns to firms as spending in the circular flow.
keyTerms.mi: The circular flow requires household earnings to become saving, taxes, or spending on imports.
keyTerms.cx: Household earnings return to firms as spending unless they leak out through those categories.

keyTerms.df: Leakages are saving, taxes, or spending on imports that leave the circular flow.
keyTerms.eg: Saving, taxes, and spending on imports are leakages.
keyTerms.mi: Investment, government spending, and exports are leakages from the circular flow.
keyTerms.cx: Those categories are injections that add spending back into the flow.

keyTerms.df: Injections are investment, government spending, and exports that add spending back into the flow.
keyTerms.eg: Investment, government spending, and exports are injections.
keyTerms.mi: Injections consist of saving, taxes, and spending on imports.
keyTerms.cx: Saving, taxes, and spending on imports are leakages rather than injections.

scenario.su: An analyst must classify whether the circular flow is in balance while relying on recorded totals that show total leakages equal total injections. The analyst must also account for a household spending record showing earnings returning to firms and category records listing saving, taxes, imports, investment, government spending, and exports.
scenario.ma: household spending record, leakage category record, injection category record, equal-totals notation

mc.q: A record groups saving, taxes, and spending on imports together, while another groups investment, government spending, and exports together. How should the two groups be classified in the circular flow?
op: First group leakages; second group injections
Both groups add spending back into flow
Saving and taxes belong with injections
Exports and investment belong with leakages
mc.ex: The first group contains saving, taxes, and spending on imports that leak out, while the second contains injections that add spending back. Exports and investment are injections, not leakages.

mc.q: A record shows that total leakages equal total injections. An analyst must identify both the condition of the circular flow and the direction of national income. Which conclusion follows?
op: Flow is balanced; national income neither rises nor falls
Flow is balanced; national income rises
Flow is balanced; national income falls
Flow is not in balance; income neither rises nor falls
mc.ex: Equal total leakages and total injections make the flow balanced, and national income neither rises nor falls. A balanced flow therefore does not mean that national income rises.

changeSummary: Re-authored both multiple-choice items with the uniquely supported option first and complete source-fact citations.
Replaced the duplicated wrong proposition in the second option set with distinct alternatives.
addressedDiagnoses: Removed the duplicated wrong proposition identified in the second option set.
Improved choice discriminability while preserving source fidelity and assessment correctness.

facts: A dictionary stores key-value pairs and looks up each value by its key rather than by a numeric position.
Because a dictionary looks up values using keys, it cannot hold duplicate keys.
Dictionaries are written with curly braces in key: value form and are ideal when data is naturally labeled rather than ordered.

keyTerms.df: A dictionary is a structure that stores key-value pairs and looks up values using keys.
keyTerms.eg: A Python dictionary is written with curly braces in key: value form.
keyTerms.mi: A dictionary looks up each key by its value.
keyTerms.cx: Dictionary lookup uses a key to find its associated value.

keyTerms.df: Key-value pairs associate stored values with keys used to look up those values.
keyTerms.eg: Dictionaries store key-value pairs for naturally labeled data.
keyTerms.mi: Key-value pairs require values to be found by numeric position.
keyTerms.cx: Values in key-value pairs are found using their associated keys.

keyTerms.df: Curly braces are the notation used to write dictionaries in key: value form.
keyTerms.eg: Dictionaries use curly braces around key: value form.
keyTerms.mi: Curly braces show that data is naturally ordered.
keyTerms.cx: Naturally labeled data makes dictionaries ideal, while curly braces provide their written form.

scenario.su: A dictionary is written with curly braces in key: value form, and the data is naturally labeled rather than ordered. Decide whether lookup uses a key or a numeric position, under the constraint that the dictionary cannot hold duplicate keys.
scenario.ma: curly braces in key: value form observation, naturally labeled rather than ordered data observation, lookup-by-key design

mc.q: A dictionary stores key-value pairs, and an observation contrasts lookup by a key with lookup by a numeric position; which proposition captures the supported distinction?
op: Keys are looked up using values
Numeric positions are looked up using values
Values are looked up using numeric positions
Values are looked up using keys
mc.ex: A dictionary finds each value using its associated key rather than a numeric position. Looking up keys using values reverses the stated relationship.

mc.q: A Python design uses curly braces in key: value form but presents duplicate keys; under a deadline, how should students classify it while respecting both observed details?
op: It is ideal for naturally ordered data
It is a dictionary with duplicate keys
It looks up keys by each value
It cannot be a dictionary as presented
mc.ex: A dictionary cannot hold duplicate keys because it looks up values using keys. Curly-brace key: value form does not make duplicate keys compatible with a dictionary.

changeSummary: Replaced only the diagnosed scenario with a two-sentence, source-grounded decision that removes the invented named example and states the duplicate-key constraint.
Revised the scenario materials to name multiple source-grounded observations and a lookup design for inspection.
addressedDiagnoses: Removed the invented named example "Python Data Boundary Design Lab" from the scenario while preserving all fields not implicated by the diagnosis.

facts: A conditional statement chooses which block of code to run based on whether a condition is true; if-else takes exactly one branch, and boolean operators (and, or, not) build compound conditions.
An if statement runs its body only when the condition is true, and skips it when the condition is false.
An else clause holds statements that run when the if condition is false.
and returns True only if both conditions are true; or returns True if either is true; not inverts a single condition.

keyTerms.df: A conditional statement selects a block according to whether its condition is true.
keyTerms.eg: When a condition is true, the conditional statement chooses which block runs.
keyTerms.mi: A conditional statement requires boolean operators to choose a block.
keyTerms.cx: Block selection can be based on whether a condition is true; a compound condition is not required.

keyTerms.df: An if statement is a conditional form whose body runs when its condition is true.
keyTerms.eg: When the if condition is false, the if statement skips its body.
keyTerms.mi: An if statement runs its body when its condition is false.
keyTerms.cx: A false condition leads the body to be skipped, not run.

keyTerms.df: An else clause contains statements associated with a false if condition.
keyTerms.eg: If the condition is false, the statements in the else clause run.
keyTerms.mi: An else clause holds statements for a true if condition.
keyTerms.cx: Its statements correspond to the condition being false rather than true.

scenario.su: A student must label which block runs in an if-else before a deadline, with the recorded if condition marked false. The student must also distinguish a compound condition recorded as true or false, using the noted and, or, and not operators.
scenario.ma: if condition notation marked false, if-body observation marked skipped, else-clause observation marked run, and-or-not condition table marked true or false

mc.q: An if condition is observed as false, and its else clause holds statements. Which result correctly identifies the if body and the else statements?
op: Running if body; skipped else statements
Skipped if body; skipped else statements
Running if body; running else statements
Skipped if body; running else statements
mc.ex: A false if condition makes the if statement skip its body, and the else clause holds statements that run for that false condition. A running if body with skipped else statements reverses those results.

mc.q: A compound condition records one condition as true and the other as false; students must classify both results before a deadline. Which notation correctly compares and with or?
op: and and or are both False
and and or are both True
and is False; or is True
and is True; or is False
mc.ex: and returns True only when both conditions are true, while or returns True when either condition is true. They therefore do not both return True for these recorded conditions.

changeSummary: Re-authored the first multiple-choice item, including its stem, choices, key, citations, and explanation.
addressedDiagnoses: Removed the first explanation's contradiction about whether the else statements run or skip when the if condition is false.

facts: A DC circuit is a conducting path with steady current, sources, and components whose voltages and currents obey conservation rules.
Series components share the same current; parallel branches share the same voltage.
Kirchhoff's junction rule expresses charge conservation, and the loop rule expresses energy conservation.

keyTerms.df: A DC circuit is a conducting path distinguished by steady current, sources, components, and conservation rules.
keyTerms.eg: Use the term DC circuit while comparing series components that share the same current with parallel branches that share the same voltage.
keyTerms.mi: A DC circuit has component voltages and currents that oppose conservation rules.
keyTerms.cx: Its component voltages and currents obey conservation rules along the conducting path.

keyTerms.df: Series components are circuit components distinguished by sharing the same current.
keyTerms.eg: Two series components in a DC circuit carry the same current.
keyTerms.mi: Series components are identified by sharing the same voltage.
keyTerms.cx: Shared current characterizes series components, while shared voltage characterizes parallel branches.

keyTerms.df: The junction rule is a Kirchhoff rule that expresses charge conservation.
keyTerms.eg: Kirchhoff's junction rule and loop rule express charge and energy conservation, respectively.
keyTerms.mi: The junction rule expresses energy conservation rather than charge conservation.
keyTerms.cx: Charge conservation corresponds to the junction rule; energy conservation corresponds to the loop rule.

scenario.su: Students must label a conducting path as a DC circuit and distinguish its series components from its parallel branches before a deadline. The steady-current notation, component current comparison, and branch voltage comparison must support one defensible classification despite the time constraint.
scenario.ma: steady-current path diagram, component current comparison, branch voltage comparison

mc.q: A circuit notation shows equal current through series components and equal voltage across parallel branches; which comparison correctly distinguishes the two observed component relations?
op: Series and parallel components share voltage
Series share current; parallel branches share voltage
Series and parallel branches share current
Series share voltage; parallel branches share current
mc.ex: Series components share the same current, whereas parallel branches share the same voltage. The reversed comparison incorrectly exchanges these two relations.

mc.q: A student compares junction notation tied to charge conservation with loop notation tied to energy conservation; which labels fit the records before the workshop deadline?
op: Junction and loop: charge conservation
Junction and loop: energy conservation
Junction: charge conservation; loop: energy conservation
Junction: energy conservation; loop: charge conservation
mc.ex: The junction rule expresses charge conservation, and the loop rule expresses energy conservation. Assigning energy to the junction and charge to the loop reverses the supported labels.

changeSummary: Rewrote only the first key-term example as a bounded application grounded in the supplied claims.
addressedDiagnoses: Resolved the compiler finding that the first key-term example repeated its definition.

facts: Electric current is the rate at which charge passes through a surface.
Conventional current direction is the direction positive charge would move.
Microscopic drift speed is slow even though the electric signal through a circuit propagates rapidly.

keyTerms.df: Electric current is a rate quantity defined by charge passing through a surface.
keyTerms.eg: Classify a rate for charge passing through a surface as electric current.
keyTerms.mi: Electric current names the surface through which charge passes.
keyTerms.cx: The surface marks where passage occurs; current describes the rate of that passage.

keyTerms.df: Conventional current direction identifies the direction in which positive charge would move.
keyTerms.eg: Positive charge would move in the conventional current direction.
keyTerms.mi: Conventional current direction is the rate at which positive charge passes.
keyTerms.cx: It specifies possible positive-charge motion in a direction rather than measuring passage rate.

keyTerms.df: Microscopic drift speed is slow compared with the rapidly propagating electric signal through a circuit.
keyTerms.eg: A circuit comparison pairs slow microscopic drift speed with rapid electric-signal propagation.
keyTerms.mi: Microscopic drift speed propagates rapidly while the electric signal is slow.
keyTerms.cx: The rapid propagation belongs to the electric signal, while microscopic drift remains slow.

scenario.su: A workshop group must assign accurate labels to four statements about charge, direction, drift speed, and signal propagation. The group faces a deadline and must distinguish the paired ideas using the stated observations rather than treating their properties as interchangeable.
scenario.ma: charge-through-surface rate notation, positive-charge direction notation, slow-drift observation, rapid-signal observation

mc.q: A comparison records charge passing through a surface at a rate and separately marks the direction positive charge would move. Which distinction correctly labels electric current and conventional current direction?
op: Current gives charge-passage rate; conventional direction tracks positive charge
Current tracks positive charge; conventional direction gives passage rate
Current gives positive-charge direction; conventional direction marks surface
Current marks the surface; conventional direction gives charge rate
mc.ex: Electric current is the rate of charge passing through a surface, whereas conventional current direction follows the direction positive charge would move. The two relations should not be exchanged between rate and direction.

mc.q: In a circuit comparison, the recorded microscopic drift speed is slow while the observed electric signal propagates rapidly. Under a constraint requiring one accurate paired label, which notation is supported?
op: Drift speed is slow; electric signal propagates rapidly
Drift speed is rapid; electric signal propagates slowly
Drift speed is rapid; electric signal propagates rapidly
Drift speed is slow; electric signal propagates slowly
mc.ex: Microscopic drift speed is slow even though the electric signal through a circuit propagates rapidly. Rapid propagation therefore describes the signal, not the microscopic drift speed.

changeSummary: Replaced the rejected Electric current example with a source-bounded classification application while preserving all fields not implicated by the compiler issue.
addressedDiagnoses: Resolved lesson-6:key-term-1:example-repeats-definition; the anonymous judge diagnoses listed no winner critical defects.

facts: An electric field describes the electric force per unit positive test charge at each point in space.
The direction of the electric field is the direction a positive test charge would accelerate.
Field-line density indicates relative field strength.

keyTerms.df: An electric field is a description of electric force per unit positive test charge at each point in space.
keyTerms.eg: For points in space with different field-line density, use the density to compare relative field strength.
keyTerms.mi: The electric field points opposite the direction a positive test charge would accelerate.
keyTerms.cx: Its direction agrees with the positive test charge's acceleration direction, rather than opposing it.

keyTerms.df: A positive test charge is the charge for which electric force per unit charge describes the electric field.
keyTerms.eg: The charge's acceleration direction identifies the direction of the electric field at a point in space.
keyTerms.mi: Field-line density gives the direction a positive test charge would accelerate.
keyTerms.cx: Acceleration direction establishes field direction; density instead indicates relative field strength.

keyTerms.df: Field-line density is the field-line property that indicates relative field strength.
keyTerms.eg: Comparing density at two points in space provides a comparison of relative field strength.
keyTerms.mi: Relative field strength indicates field-line density.
keyTerms.cx: The stated relation runs from the density of field lines to comparative strength, not in reverse.

scenario.su: A student must label two electric-field descriptions before a deadline, using a direction record and a field-line-density comparison. One description records where a positive test charge would accelerate, while the other compares denser and less dense field lines, so each label must follow the relevant relation.
scenario.ma: positive-test-charge acceleration direction record, denser-versus-less-dense field-line comparison, electric-force-per-unit-positive-test-charge passage

mc.q: At one point in space, a record gives electric force per unit positive test charge and an arrow gives the positive test charge's acceleration direction; what distinction is supported?
op: Field describes acceleration; direction follows force per charge
Field describes force per charge; direction follows acceleration
Field describes force per charge; direction omitted
Direction describes force per charge; field follows acceleration
mc.ex: The electric field describes electric force per unit positive test charge, while its direction follows the positive test charge's acceleration direction. Swapping those relations incorrectly makes acceleration describe the field itself.

mc.q: Two field-line displays differ in density, with the first visibly denser than the second; under a deadline, which comparison should the student record from that observation?
op: Second has greater relative field strength
First has greater relative field strength
Second describes force per positive charge
First has the positive charge direction
mc.ex: Field-line density indicates relative field strength, so the denser first display supports greater relative strength. Assigning greater strength to the less dense second display reverses the supplied relation.

changeSummary: Changed only keyTerms[0].eg to replace the definition-repeating example with a distinct source-grounded application.

facts: Capacitance is the ratio of stored charge to potential difference for a conductor or capacitor.
A capacitor stores energy in the electric field between its conductors.
For a parallel-plate capacitor, increasing plate area increases capacitance and increasing separation decreases capacitance.

keyTerms.df: Capacitance is a ratio relating stored charge to potential difference for a conductor or capacitor.
keyTerms.eg: For a conductor, stored charge is compared with potential difference.
keyTerms.mi: Capacitance is the energy stored between a capacitor's conductors.
keyTerms.cx: Energy is stored in the electric field; the charge-to-potential-difference relation identifies capacitance.

keyTerms.df: The electric field between a capacitor's conductors is where the capacitor stores energy.
keyTerms.eg: A capacitor passage associates stored energy with the region between its conductors.
keyTerms.mi: The electric field is the ratio of stored charge to potential difference.
keyTerms.cx: That ratio describes capacitance, whereas stored energy is associated with the field between conductors.

keyTerms.df: Plate area is a property whose increase raises capacitance for a parallel-plate capacitor.
keyTerms.eg: A design increases plate area and separation, invoking opposite stated relations to capacitance.
keyTerms.mi: Increasing plate area decreases capacitance in a parallel-plate capacitor.
keyTerms.cx: For parallel plates, a rise in area goes with a rise, rather than a fall, in capacitance.

scenario.su: A workshop team must label which parallel-plate design change supports increased capacitance and which supports decreased capacitance before a review deadline. One design increases plate area while another increases separation, so the team must resolve the opposing labels from the recorded changes.
scenario.ma: parallel-plate design A notation showing increased plate area, parallel-plate design B notation showing increased separation, capacitance label record

mc.q: A record identifies capacitance by comparing stored charge with potential difference, while a passage identifies where a capacitor stores energy; which paired description matches these observations?
op: Capacitance is stored charge; capacitor energy is potential difference
Capacitance is potential difference; capacitor energy is stored charge
Capacitance is the ratio; capacitor energy is field-stored
Capacitance is field-stored; capacitor energy is the ratio
mc.ex: Capacitance is the ratio of stored charge to potential difference, and a capacitor stores energy in the electric field between its conductors. The closest distractor reverses these relationships: capacitance is not field-stored energy, and capacitor energy is not the ratio.

mc.q: Design A increases plate area, while design B increases plate separation; with both changes fixed and requiring separate capacitance labels, which paired classification is supported?
op: Area increase lowers capacitance; separation increase lowers it
Area increase lowers capacitance; separation increase raises it
Area increase raises capacitance; separation increase raises it
Area increase raises capacitance; separation increase lowers it
mc.ex: For a parallel-plate capacitor, increased plate area increases capacitance and increased separation decreases it. Treating increased separation as raising capacitance reverses its stated relation.

changeSummary: Re-authored the complete first multiple-choice item to remove the overlapping ratio distractor while preserving its source-fact citations and required answer index.
addressedDiagnoses: Resolved the diagnosed ambiguity in the first question by making each paired option express a distinct relationship.

facts: Functional harmony classifies chords by the role they play in a progression, especially tonic, dominant, and pre-dominant functions.
The tonic is built on scale degree one, while pre-dominants are built on degrees two, three, four, and six.
In minor, raising the third of the fifth-degree chord makes it major and strengthens its dominant function.

keyTerms.df: Functional harmony is a classification of chords according to their roles in a progression.
keyTerms.eg: A progression classified with tonic, dominant, and pre-dominant functions uses functional harmony.
keyTerms.mi: Functional harmony classifies chords by scale degree rather than their role in a progression.
keyTerms.cx: The classification depends on each chord's role in the progression, not a replacement of role by scale degree.

keyTerms.df: The tonic is a chord function distinguished by being built on scale degree one.
keyTerms.eg: In a progression, the scale-degree-one chord receives the tonic label.
keyTerms.mi: A chord built on scale degree four has tonic function.
keyTerms.cx: Degree four supports a pre-dominant classification, while degree one supports the tonic classification.

keyTerms.df: Dominant function is the role strengthened when a minor fifth-degree chord has its third raised.
keyTerms.eg: In minor, the raised-third fifth-degree chord becomes major.
keyTerms.mi: Raising the third of the fifth-degree chord weakens its dominant function.
keyTerms.cx: The raised third strengthens the chord's dominant role instead of weakening it.

scenario.su: A progression contains two chord notations: one chord is built on scale degree one, and one chord is built on scale degree four. Decide which chord has tonic function and which has pre-dominant function; the classification must use each displayed scale degree.
scenario.ma: Inspect the scale-degree-one chord notation and the scale-degree-four chord notation, recording the displayed scale degree and the selected tonic or pre-dominant label for each.

mc.q: An editor observes one chord built on scale degree one and another on degree four; which comparison correctly distinguishes their tonic and pre-dominant functions?
op: Degree one is tonic; degree four is pre-dominant
Degree four is tonic; degree one is pre-dominant
Degrees one and four are pre-dominant functions
Degrees one and four are tonic functions
mc.ex: The tonic is built on degree one, while degree four is among the degrees supporting pre-dominants. Assigning tonic to degree four and pre-dominant to degree one reverses these supplied relationships.

mc.q: In minor, an analyst observes that the third of a fifth-degree chord was raised and must classify the resulting chord and function before a deadline; which decision fits?
op: Classify it as major with strengthened dominant function
